title: Pressure-boundary work went back into service without a test to design pressure, because no procedure required one

reason: Independent check added to the existing permit rather than a new form

title: The malfunction notification was never closed or reviewed, so the last administrative check before return to service did not happen
Repeat failures of the same seal were treated as routine repairs, not as a reliability warning
The management-of-change procedure existed on paper but had not been used since 2018
The emergency plan named the major-leak scenario but gave no isolation criteria and no delegated authority to isolate
When the vapour cloud blocked access, the shift response stayed on 'find the leak' rather than switching to upstream isolation
Emergency isolation valves could only be closed by hand at the valve, inside the area the release made unreachable
Gas detection only displayed an alarm; it did not trigger shutdown or protection, and it alarmed after people had already seen the cloud
A damaged flameproof light fitting stayed in service in a hazardous area under breakdown-led electrical maintenance
Control-room staff held emergency duties after a four-day general course, with no defined qualification or simulator practice
reason: Simulator time shared with a sister site

title: People saw the release first, but their warnings reached the control room late and diluted
One panning camera was the only view of the skid; it gave intermittent coverage and was lost seconds after ignition
Pressure transmitters at the leak point sent no data, and control-room clocks disagreed by up to 12 minutes
A calibration setting on the failed meter was changed and reversed without any record or checklist
Known pipe-wall loss was measured but not acted on: no corrective plan for three years, and painting used as the fix
The four-year thickness inspection cycle slipped to six years, and original baseline data and pipe schedules were missing
The metering P&ID was a lost original replaced by an unapproved vendor drawing that did not match the field
Safety audits used generic checklists and recorded compliance without site data, so they could not find plant-specific defects
External-audit recommendations were extended without the required approval, so overdue safety actions had no accountable owner
Maintenance notifications were treated as work permits, permits went missing untracked, and job safety plans were absent
Three of four diesel fire-water pumps were unavailable or unreliable; electric pumps happened to carry the incident
Fire drill records held no actions or observations, so drills could not show whether readiness was improving
reason: Covered by the corporate drill standard now in revision
